items.stem: Define the term 'local area network (LAN)'.
items.answer: A network covering a small geographical area, such as one building or site, usually owned by the organisation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: A network covering a small geographical area, such as one building or site, usually owned by the organisation. [2]

items.stem: Explain two differences between a LAN and a WAN.
items.answer: A LAN covers a small area such as one building while a WAN covers a large area such as a country; a LAN is usually owned by the organisation while WAN links are often leased from telecoms companies; LANs are usually faster.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark difference, explained). [4]

items.stem: Explain why a network interface card is needed.
items.answer: It provides the physical connection to the network and has a unique MAC address so data can be delivered to the correct device.
items.markingKey: 1 mark connection; 1 mark MAC address/identification. [2]

items.stem: Jonas is installing a network in a small office for GreenLeaf Pharmacy in Lagos. Describe the role of a router and of a switch in this network.
items.answer: Router: connects the LAN to the internet/other networks, forwarding packets by IP address. Switch: connects devices within the LAN, sending data to the correct device by MAC address.
items.markingKey: 1 mark router; 1 mark switch. [2]

items.stem: Harbour Bank has offices in Singapore and Istanbul and wants staff in both offices to share files. (a) Describe the role of a router and of a switch in this network. (b) Explain one disadvantage of networking the computers.
items.answer: (a) Router: connects the LAN to the internet/other networks, forwarding packets by IP address. Switch: connects devices within the LAN, sending data to the correct device by MAC address. (b) Viruses can spread; security risks; cost of equipment and technicians; if the server/switch fails many users are affected.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark router; 1 mark switch. [2] (b) 1 mark point; 1 mark explanation. [2]

items.stem: Riverside Medical Centre in Madrid is setting up a network for 60 staff in one building, with access to the internet. Discuss whether Riverside Medical Centre should use a wireless network instead of a cabled network.
items.answer: Points for: mobility; easy to add devices; no cabling costs or disruption. Points against / limitations: slower and less reliable; interference; security risks from interception; limited range. Conclusion: many organisations use cables for fixed computers and wireless for mobile devices.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks points developed and applied with a conclusion. Indicative content — for: mobility; easy to add devices; no cabling costs or disruption. Against: slower and less reliable; interference; security risks from interception; limited range. Conclusion may argue: many organisations use cables for fixed computers and wireless for mobile devices. [4]

items.stem: State what is meant by 'wide area network (WAN)'.
items.answer: A network covering a large geographical area, connecting LANs, often using telecommunications links owned by other companies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: A network covering a large geographical area, connecting LANs, often using telecommunications links owned by other companies. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between 'local area network (LAN)' and 'switch'.
items.answer: local area network (LAN): A network covering a small geographical area, such as one building or site, usually owned by the organisation. switch: Connects devices within a LAN and sends data only to the device it is addressed to, using MAC addresses.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: local area network (LAN) correctly described; 1 mark: switch correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Describe the difference between 'wireless access point (WAP)' and 'local area network (LAN)'.
items.answer: wireless access point (WAP): Allows wireless devices to connect to a wired network. local area network (LAN): A network covering a small geographical area, such as one building or site, usually owned by the organisation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: wireless access point (WAP) correctly described; 1 mark: local area network (LAN) correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Explain why transfer speeds are given in bits per second while file sizes are given in bytes.
items.answer: Data is transmitted one bit at a time over a link, so speed is measured in bits; files are stored in bytes; to calculate times, bytes must be multiplied by 8.
items.markingKey: 1 mark bits transmitted serially; 1 mark multiply by 8 to convert. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between 'internet' and 'wireless access point (WAP)'.
items.answer: internet: A worldwide network of interconnected networks that communicate using the TCP/IP protocols. wireless access point (WAP): Allows wireless devices to connect to a wired network.

items.answer: website: A collection of related web pages on the World Wide Web, accessed using a URL. extranet: Part of an organisation's intranet that authorised outside users, such as suppliers or customers, can access over the internet.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: website correctly described; 1 mark: extranet correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why information found using a search engine may not be reliable. (b) Describe two ways to refine a search to get more relevant results.
items.answer: (a) Anyone can publish on the web; results are ranked by popularity or advertising, not accuracy; pages may be out of date or biased. (b) Use quotation marks for exact phrases; use AND/OR/NOT (or −) operators; use advanced search filters such as date, site or file type.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per point, max 3. [3] (b) 1 mark each, max 2. [2]

items.stem: Arjun found information on a website about health care in Hanoi. Describe 2 checks Arjun could make to decide whether the information is reliable, explaining why each helps.
items.answer: Check whether sources and references are given — so facts can be checked; Check the domain, e.g. .gov or .ac — government and academic sites are more likely to be reliable
items.markingKey: 1 mark per check, 1 mark per explanation, e.g. the author and organisation responsible for the site (to judge expertise and possible bias); the date the page was last updated (to check the information is current); the domain, e.g. .gov or .ac (government and academic sites are more likely to be reliable); whether sources and references are given (so facts can be checked); whether the same facts appear on other reliable sites (cross-referencing confirms accuracy); the spelling, grammar and presence of adverts (poor quality or heavy advertising may indicate an unreliable or commercial site). [4]

items.stem: Freya found information on a website about health care in Dubai. Describe 3 checks Freya could make to decide whether the information is reliable, explaining why each helps.
items.answer: Check the spelling, grammar and presence of adverts — poor quality or heavy advertising may indicate an unreliable or commercial site; Check the date the page was last updated — to check the information is current; Check whether the same facts appear on other reliable sites — cross-referencing confirms accuracy

items.stem: Hana is training staff at Meridian Hospital in Madrid to use the internet, the intranet and the extranet. Discuss whether students should rely on search engines for research rather than on books and libraries.
items.answer: Points for: fast access to vast, up-to-date information; many formats; searchable. Points against / limitations: reliability varies; information overload; ranking not by accuracy; books are edited and checked. Conclusion: search engines are valuable if students evaluate sources critically and cross-check facts.

Against: reliability varies; information overload; ranking not by accuracy; books are edited and checked. Conclusion may argue: search engines are valuable if students evaluate sources critically and cross-check facts. [4]

items.stem: Define the term 'router'.
items.answer: Forwards data packets between different networks, such as a LAN and the internet, using IP addresses.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Forwards data packets between different networks, such as a LAN and the internet, using IP addresses. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between 'wide area network (WAN)' and 'local area network (LAN)'.
items.answer: wide area network (WAN): A network covering a large geographical area, connecting LANs, often using telecommunications links owned by other companies. local area network (LAN): A network covering a small geographical area, such as one building or site, usually owned by the organisation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: wide area network (WAN) correctly described; 1 mark: local area network (LAN) correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between 'wireless access point (WAP)' and 'router'.
items.answer: wireless access point (WAP): Allows wireless devices to connect to a wired network. router: Forwards data packets between different networks, such as a LAN and the internet, using IP addresses.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: wireless access point (WAP) correctly described; 1 mark: router correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Which network device connects two LANs that use the same protocol so they behave as one network?
items.answer: Bridge
items.markingKey: bridge: connects two LANs that use the same protocol so they behave as one network.

items.stem: Arjun is installing a network in a small office for Palm Grove Hotel in Lisbon. State whether a LAN or a WAN is needed, giving a reason.
items.answer: LAN for one building/site; WAN to connect offices in different cities.
items.markingKey: 1 mark choice; 1 mark reason. [2]

items.stem: A 5 MB database backup is sent over a connection with a speed of 10 Mbps. Using 1 MB = 1 000 000 bytes, 1 Mbps = 1 000 000 bits per second, calculate the time taken to transfer the file. Show your working.
items.answer: 4 seconds

items.stem: Eagles Sports Club has offices in Bangkok and Bogotá and wants staff in both offices to share files. Discuss whether Eagles Sports Club should use a wireless network instead of a cabled network.
items.answer: Points for: mobility; easy to add devices; no cabling costs or disruption. Points against / limitations: slower and less reliable; interference; security risks from interception; limited range. Conclusion: many organisations use cables for fixed computers and wireless for mobile devices.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks developed points on one or both sides; 5-6 marks balanced, applied discussion with a justified conclusion. Indicative content — for: mobility; easy to add devices; no cabling costs or disruption. Against: slower and less reliable; interference; security risks from interception; limited range. Conclusion may argue: many organisations use cables for fixed computers and wireless for mobile devices. [6]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain what is meant by the term 'video conferencing'. (b) Define the term 'carbon copy (CC) / blind carbon copy (BCC)'.
items.answer: (a) Communication in which people in different places see and hear each other in real time using cameras, microphones, screens and a network. (b) Email fields that send copies of a message to other recipients; BCC recipients are hidden from the others.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. items.stem: Distinguish between 'carbon copy (CC) / blind carbon copy (BCC)' and 'instant messaging (IM)'.
items.answer: carbon copy (CC) / blind carbon copy (BCC): Email fields that send copies of a message to other recipients; BCC recipients are hidden from the others. instant messaging (IM): Real-time text communication between users who are online, often with presence information showing who is available.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: carbon copy (CC) / blind carbon copy (BCC) correctly described; 1 mark: instant messaging (IM) correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between 'carbon copy (CC) / blind carbon copy (BCC)' and 'video conferencing'.

items.stem: Orbit Games Studio has teams in Colombo and Mumbai who need to communicate every day. Explain how the organisation can protect itself from phishing emails.
items.answer: Train staff to recognise phishing; spam filters; never click unknown links; verify requests by phone.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point, max 2. [2]

items.stem: A video conference between 5 offices lasts 45 minutes. Each office sends a video stream of 1200 kbps (1 kbps = 1000 bits per second) and receives the streams of all the other offices. Calculate (a) the download bandwidth each office needs in kbps and (b) the total data received by one office in MB (1 MB = 1 000 000 bytes).

Zara manages a project at Palm Grove Hotel in Dubai with partners overseas. (a) Explain when instant messaging would be more suitable than email. (b) Explain how the organisation can protect itself from phishing emails.
items.answer: (a) For quick, informal questions when the other person is online and an immediate answer is needed. (b) Train staff to recognise phishing; spam filters; never click unknown links; verify requests by phone.

items.stem: Sunrise Bakery has teams in Lagos and Riyadh who need to communicate every day. (a) Explain two disadvantages of video conferencing. (b) Explain how the organisation can protect itself from phishing emails.
items.answer: (a) Time zones; lag/poor quality with low bandwidth; cost of equipment; lack of personal contact; security of calls. (b) Train staff to recognise phishing; spam filters; never click unknown links; verify requests by phone.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Define the term 'website'. (b) Define the term 'intranet'.
items.answer: (a) A collection of related web pages on the World Wide Web, accessed using a URL. (b) A private network within an organisation, using internet technologies, that can only be accessed by the organisation's members.

items.stem: Describe the difference between 'search engine' and 'website'.
items.answer: search engine: Software that searches an index of web pages for given keywords and returns a ranked list of results. website: A collection of related web pages on the World Wide Web, accessed using a URL.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: search engine correctly described; 1 mark: website correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Describe two ways to refine a search to get more relevant results. (b) Explain two differences between an intranet and the internet.
items.answer: (a) Use quotation marks for exact phrases; use AND/OR/NOT (or −) operators; use advanced search filters such as date, site or file type. (b) An intranet is private to an organisation while the internet is public; intranet content is controlled and more reliable; an intranet is usually behind a firewall with login needed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each, max 2. [2] (b) 2 × (1 mark difference, explained). [4]

items.stem: Harbour Bank in Nairobi wants to share policies and forms with its staff and let its suppliers check orders. (a) Explain the difference between an intranet and an extranet. (b) Explain one advantage of an intranet for the organisation.
items.answer: (a) Intranet: private to staff; extranet: gives authorised external users (suppliers, customers) access to part of it. (b) Information is shared in one place, up to date and only accessible to staff, which is more secure and reliable.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each. [2] (b) 1 mark point; 1 mark explanation. [2]

items.stem: SkyLink Airways in Doha wants to share policies and forms with its staff and let its suppliers check orders. (a) Describe three things to check when judging whether a website is reliable. (b) Describe how a search engine finds and ranks web pages.
items.answer: (a) Author/organisation; date updated; domain type; references; cross-check with other sites; bias/advertising; spelling. (b) Web crawlers follow links and index pages; keywords in the query are matched to the index; results ranked using relevance and links/popularity.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each, max 3. [3] (b) 1 mark crawl/index; 1 mark match; 1 mark ranking. [3]
